content: 1. The use of the drug ded is currently reserved for second-line therapy but may be considered in the future if a generic pediatric formulation becomes available. 2. Darunavir/ritonavir (DRV/r) is an option for third-line therapy in settings where it is accessible. 3. Unboosted protease inhibitors (PIs) such as fosamprenavir (FPV), darunavir (DRV), and atazanavir (ATV), as well as other PIs like indinavir/ritonavir (IDV/r), saquinavir/ritonavir (SQV/r), fosamprenavir/ritonavir (FPV/r), and tipranavir/ritonavir (TPV/r), are associated with reduced viral suppression, high pill burden, and/or a higher frequency of side effects. Therefore, their use is discouraged. 4. The sequencing of nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) was evaluated for both protease inhibitor (PI) and non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI) failures, with the goal of maximizing antiviral activity while considering resistance mutation selection. 5. If a thymidine analogue NRTI drug (e.g., zidovudine [AZT] or stavudine [d4T]) was used in a failing first-line regimen, abacavir (ABC) or tenofovir (TDF) should be used in the second-line regimen. 6. Conversely, if a non-thymidine analogue NRTI drug (e.g., ABC or TDF) was used in a failing first-line regimen, AZT should be used in the second-line regimen. 7. The use of didanosine (ddI) in second-line regimens is no longer recommended. Instead, continuing lamivudine (3TC) is preferred, even in cases where 3TC resistance is likely. 8. HIV harboring 3TC resistance with the M184V mutation may exhibit reduced viral replication capacity and may induce some degree of resensitization to AZT or TDF, as suggested by in vitro data. 9. More evidence is needed to guide the selection of second-line regimens, particularly for young children whose first-line lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r)-based regimen has failed. 10. Validation studies are critical to assess simplified dosing for atazanavir/ritonavir (ATV/r) and darunavir/ritonavir (DRV/r) fixed-dose combinations (FDCs) to ensure the availability of effective alternatives. 11. Innovative second-line strategies, such as combining a protease inhibitor (PI) with an integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI) or using induction and maintenance approaches with boosted PI monotherapy, should be explored in children. 12. Further studies are needed to evaluate the role and feasibility of genotyping to inform second-line regimen choices in public health settings. 13. National programs should develop policies for third-line antiretroviral therapy (ART), although the evidence supporting these recommendations is of low quality. 14. Third-line regimens should include new drugs with minimal risk of cross-resistance to previously used regimens, such as INSTIs, second-generation NNRTIs, and PIs. 15. Patients on failing second-line regimens with no new antiretroviral drug options should continue with a tolerated regimen, as this is a conditional recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 16. In 2010, the World Health Organization (WHO) issued recommendations on third-line ART in the context of limited evidence for treating patients whose second-line therapy had failed. 17. Cohort data from that time showed high mortality rates among individuals for whom second-line ART had failed. 18. Salvage regimens were recommended to include new drugs such as DRV/r, etravirine (ETV), and raltegravir (RAL), with or without previously used antiretrovirals that retained residual virological activity, particularly from the NRTI class. 19. These recommendations were maintained in 2013 based on additional trial data, but the need for more clinical and operational research to guide third-line ART strategies was emphasized. 20. Recent data from randomized controlled trials and observational cohorts support the efficacy of DRV/r-, ETV-, dolutegravir (DTG)-, and RAL-containing regimens in treatment-experienced adults, although most studies were conducted in middleto high-income settings. 21. Many of these antiretroviral drugs have shown efficacy in prospective studies involving children and adolescents. 22. The data support the efficacy of new agents such as INSTIs, second-generation PIs, and NNRTIs in individuals for whom second-line ART has failed. 23. However, in ART-experienced patients with multiple NRTI resistance mutations, there is uncertainty about whether maintaining or recycling previously used NRTIs provides clinical benefit. 24. NRTI agents are often associated with cumulative toxicity, and their inclusion in third-line ART may increase pill burden and the risk of drug interactions. 25. Avoiding NRTIs in third-line regimens is now more feasible due to the availability of new antiretroviral drug classes with different resistance profiles. 26. Comparative studies suggest that NRTI-sparing regimens may have better tolerability, but further evidence is needed in highly treatment-experienced patients. 27. WHO's 2013 recommendations for third-line ART were maintained in 2015 due to limited evidence supporting the equivalence of NRTI-sparing regimens to NRTI-containing salvage regimens. 28. Further research is needed on the pharmacokinetics, safety, and efficacy of salvage regimens in children, adolescents, and pregnant women. 29. Countries must balance the need to develop policies for third-line ART with the continued expansion and optimal use of firstand second-line ART. 30. Financial constraints in many countries may limit the adoption of third-line regimens, as these drugs are often more expensive or their costs are not well-established. 31. Strategies for third-line ART in resource-limited settings require further research, including studies on simplified dosing, heat-stable formulations, and the safety of new drugs in children, adolescents, and pregnant women. 32. Pharmacovigilance research is needed to assess the long-term safety of antiretroviral drugs and their interactions with treatments for tuberculosis, malaria, hepatitis, and opioid substitution therapy. 33. Pilot studies are urgently needed to implement third-line ART in resource-limited settings with constrained capacity and resources. 34. Special considerations are required for children, adolescents, and pregnant women, as there is limited data on the use of newer antiretroviral drugs in these populations. 35. Dolutegravir (DTG) is currently approved for adolescents aged 12 years and older, but its availability is expected to be limited. 36. Darunavir (DRV) cannot be used in children younger than 3 years and is only available as a single drug through a donation program in selected countries. 37. The IMPAACT 1093 study is underway to determine the safety and dosing of DTG in younger children, with results expected to support pediatric registration by regulatory agencies. 38. For pregnant women, DTG should only be used if clearly indicated due to the lack of well-controlled studies and pharmacokinetic data during pregnancy. 39. Research gaps include the need for studies on the pharmacokinetics, safety, and efficacy of third-line regimens in children, adolescents, and pregnant women. 40. The Antiretroviral Pregnancy Registry currently reports limited in-utero exposure data for INSTIs, but this is expected to increase with expanded use of DTG as a first-line therapy. 41. There is no evidence of fetal toxicity with INSTIs based on animal studies, but further research is needed to confirm safety in pregnant women. 42. For DRV, no increased risk of birth defects has been reported to date, despite sufficient first-trimester exposure data to detect such risks. 43. Pilot studies are urgently needed to implement third-line ART in resource-limited settings with constrained capacity and resources.
